prompt: Scientist 1 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.text: The bridge's motion grew because walkers synchronized their steps with it.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 describes a feedback loop in which walkers fall into step with the motion and amplify it.

choices.text: Adding fins to the bridge deck would be the correct way to eliminate the sway.
choices.rationale: Fins are Scientist 2's proposed fix for wind-driven motion.

choices.text: The sway would occur on a windy day even with no one on the bridge.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 notes that no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.

choices.text: The crowd's footsteps were a response to the sway rather than its cause.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's view of the footsteps.

explanation: Scientist 1's explanation is that synchronized footsteps drive and amplify the sway.

stimulus.title: The Swaying Footbridge
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The bridge swayed from side to side on its opening day because of the people walking on it. When a crowd walks across a flexible bridge, small sideways movements make people adjust their steps to keep their balance. Many walkers end up stepping in time with the sway, and their combined footsteps push the bridge at exactly the frequency at which it naturally rocks. The more the bridge moves, the more people fall into step, so the motion grows. The sway appeared only when the crowd was large and stopped within minutes when the crowd was cleared, and no sway has been measured on windy days when the bridge was empty.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The sway was caused by wind. As wind flows past the bridge deck and cables, it sheds swirling eddies alternately from each side, producing a push that switches direction at a regular rate. If that rate matches a natural frequency of the bridge, the structure rocks in resonance. The opening day was breezy, and the deck's flat shape is well suited to shedding eddies. Pedestrians certainly felt the motion and reacted to it, but their steps were a response to the sway, not its cause. Adding fins to the deck to break up the eddies, rather than limiting the crowd, is the correct fix.

prompt: Despite their disagreement, both scientists would accept that:

choices.text: yellow pigments are present in leaves before autumn begins.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says yellow pigments are present all along; Scientist 2 concedes yellow may be unmasked.

choices.text: red pigments protect the cells of a leaf from excess light.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 makes this claim.

choices.text: a leaf's autumn color provides no benefit at all to the tree.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 argues that red color is beneficial.

choices.text: the tree makes new pigments in its leaves as autumn begins.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the colors are revealed, not made.

explanation: Both allow that yellow is unmasked; the dispute is over red.

stimulus.title: The Colors of Autumn
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The red and yellow colors of autumn leaves are simply revealed, not made. Throughout summer a leaf is packed with green chlorophyll, which hides yellow and orange pigments that are present all along and help capture light. As days shorten, the tree stops repairing chlorophyll and breaks it down to recover its nitrogen, and the green fades. The yellow pigments remain and finally show. Red colors come from the breakdown of sugars trapped in the leaf once the tree seals off the leaf stem. The display is a side effect of recycling, which is why a leaf's color has no clear benefit to the tree.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Red autumn leaves are produced on purpose. The red pigments, called anthocyanins, are not present in summer; the leaf makes them fresh in autumn, using energy and sugar at a time when the tree is shutting down. Making them would be wasteful unless they did something useful. Anthocyanins absorb excess light and protect the leaf's cells while the tree pulls valuable nutrients out of the leaf before it drops. Leaves on the sunny side of a tree turn redder than shaded leaves, and trees growing in poor soil, which need to recover nutrients most, produce the reddest leaves. Yellow pigments may be unmasked, but red is manufactured.

prompt: Which of the following observations, if confirmed, would provide the strongest support for Scientist 1's explanation?

choices.text: Young perch caged near the lake bottom in August die within days, while those caged near the surface survive.
choices.rationale: Correct. This directly shows that bottom-water conditions kill young perch, the mechanism Scientist 1 proposes.

choices.text: Perch populations in nearby lakes that have farms and blooms but no zander are found to be increasing.
choices.rationale: Healthy perch where zander are absent supports Scientist 2.

choices.text: The number of zander in Miller Lake is found to have doubled over the past two years, while perch counts fell.
choices.rationale: Growing zander numbers support Scientist 2's predation explanation.

choices.text: Oxygen levels near the lake bottom in August are found to be the same as they were thirty years ago, before the decline.
choices.rationale: Unchanged oxygen levels would undercut the idea that oxygen loss caused a recent decline.

explanation: Scientist 1's mechanism is suffocation of young perch in low-oxygen bottom water; a cage experiment showing exactly that is the strongest support.

stimulus.title: The Perch of Miller Lake
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The decline of perch in Miller Lake began soon after the farms upstream expanded. Fertilizer washed into the lake by rain feeds algae, which bloom across the surface each summer. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Measurements taken in August show oxygen levels near the bottom of the lake that are too low for perch eggs and young fish to survive. Adult perch can move to shallower water, but their young cannot, so each year fewer fish reach adulthood. Reducing fertilizer runoff would allow the oxygen to recover and the perch population to rebuild.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The perch decline is due to the arrival of the zander, a predatory fish first recorded in Miller Lake eight years ago, probably released by anglers. Zander feed heavily on young perch, and their numbers have grown each year while the perch count has fallen. Low oxygen alone cannot explain the pattern: the lake had algae blooms for decades before perch began to decline, and nearby lakes with similar farms and blooms still have healthy perch populations but no zander. Stomach samples from zander in the lake contain mostly young perch. Removing zander by netting would allow the perch to recover even if the fertilizer runoff continued.

prompt: Suppose the bridge swayed strongly one calm, windless evening while a large crowd crossed it. This observation would most likely:

choices.text: weaken both viewpoints to the same degree.
choices.rationale: The observation is exactly what Scientist 1 predicts.

choices.text: support Scientist 1's viewpoint and weaken Scientist 2's.
choices.rationale: Correct. Sway with a crowd but no wind fits the pedestrian explanation and contradicts the wind explanation.

choices.text: support Scientist 2's viewpoint and weaken Scientist 1's.
choices.rationale: Without wind, the eddy mechanism cannot operate.

choices.text: support both viewpoints about equally.
choices.rationale: The observation contradicts the wind explanation.

explanation: No wind removes Scientist 2's cause, while a large crowd supplies Scientist 1's cause.

prompt: The central disagreement between the two scientists concerns:

choices.text: whether zander are actually present in the waters of Miller Lake.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not deny the zander's presence; the dispute is about what matters.

choices.text: whether low oxygen or predation is responsible for the loss of young perch.
choices.rationale: Correct. Each proposes a different cause for the loss of young perch.

choices.text: whether algae blooms spread across the surface of the lake each summer.
choices.rationale: Both acknowledge the summer blooms.

choices.text: whether the number of perch in Miller Lake has actually fallen in recent years.
choices.rationale: Both accept that the perch population has declined.

explanation: The disagreement is about the cause of the decline, not about whether it is happening.

prompt: Scientist 1 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.text: Migrating in daylight would expose small songbirds to hunting hawks.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says daytime predators make a small bird in open country an easy target.

choices.text: Swallows migrate at night in order to avoid being hunted by hawks and falcons.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says swallows migrate by day and can afford the risk.

choices.text: Cooler night air keeps songbirds from overheating during long flights.
choices.rationale: Overheating is part of Scientist 2's explanation.

choices.text: Songbirds find their way mainly by the positions of the stars in the night sky.
choices.rationale: Star navigation is cited by Scientist 2.

explanation: Predator avoidance is Scientist 1's central reason for night migration.

stimulus.title: Why Songbirds Fly at Night
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Most small songbirds migrate at night because darkness protects them from predators. Hawks and falcons hunt by sight during the day, and a small bird crossing open country in daylight is an easy target. At night the hunters are roosting. Night flight also lets birds use the daylight hours to feed and rebuild the fat they burn in flight. Birds that migrate in flocks during the day, such as swallows, are fast fliers that can feed on insects while moving, so they can afford the risk. The timing of migration therefore reflects a trade-off between safety from predators and the need to eat.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Small birds migrate at night because of the physical conditions of the night sky. Night air is cooler and calmer, so a flying bird loses heat more easily and does not overheat during hours of hard flapping. Cool air also slows the loss of water from a bird's breath, which matters on long flights with nowhere to drink. The atmosphere is usually less turbulent after sunset, which lowers the energy cost of flight. Songbirds also navigate using the stars, a cue available only at night. Predators influence where birds stop to rest, but the decision to fly after dark is set by the demands of the flight itself.

choices.text: the sway was strongest at times when the bridge was empty.
choices.rationale: Neither scientist claims this; Scientist 1 says the opposite.

choices.text: the bridge rocked at one of its natural frequencies.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says footsteps matched the bridge's natural frequency; Scientist 2 describes resonance at a natural frequency.

choices.text: the size of the crowd on the bridge had no effect on the sway.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says the sway appeared only with a large crowd.

choices.text: pedestrians caused the bridge to begin rocking in the first place.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the pedestrians responded to the sway rather than causing it.

explanation: Resonance at a natural frequency appears in both explanations; they differ on what supplied the push.

prompt: Suppose each of the following were discovered. Which one would most strengthen Scientist 2's position?

choices.text: The breakdown of chlorophyll releases nitrogen that the tree stores for the following spring.
choices.rationale: Nitrogen recovery from chlorophyll is part of Scientist 1's account.

choices.text: Shaded autumn leaves give back fewer nutrients to the tree than sunlit, red leaves do.
choices.rationale: Correct. A link between red, sunlit leaves and better nutrient recovery supports the protective role Scientist 2 proposes.

choices.text: Red pigment appears in a leaf only after the tree has sealed off the leaf's stem.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 ties red color to sugars trapped after the stem is sealed, so this fits Scientist 1.

choices.text: Yellow pigments are detected in green leaves throughout the summer growing season.
choices.rationale: Both scientists accept that yellow pigments are present in summer.

explanation: Scientist 2 claims red pigments protect nutrient recovery; evidence that sunlit red leaves yield more nutrients supports that.
